column1: What is the bivalence principle in classical propositional logic?
column2: Every atomic proposition has exactly one of two truth values—true or false—with no intermediate states or gradations.

column1: What is truth-functionality, and why is it the second core invariant of propositional logic?
column2: The truth value of a compound proposition depends exclusively on the truth values of its component propositions, never on their meaning, causal relations, or content—enabling mechanical/algorithmic evaluation via truth tables.

column1: Distinguish semantic entailment (⊨) from syntactic derivability (⊢).
column2: Γ ⊨ φ means φ is true in every interpretation where Γ is true (a claim about meaning/models). Γ ⊢ φ means φ can be derived from Γ via a finite formal proof using explicit symbolic rules (a claim about mechanical construction).

column1: What does the Completeness Theorem state about classical first-order logic?
column2: Γ ⊨ φ if and only if Γ ⊢ φ — semantic entailment and syntactic derivability coincide exactly; formal proof systems capture all and only logical truths.

column1: In natural deduction, what is the difference between an introduction rule and an elimination rule?
column2: Introduction rules specify how to construct/prove a formula using a given connective (answering 'what do I need to show?'). Elimination rules specify how to extract conclusions from a formula containing that connective (answering 'what can I extract from what I have?').

column1: Why does first-order logic surpass propositional logic in expressive power?
column2: FOL decomposes atomic propositions into predicates, individual constants/variables, and quantifiers (∀, ∃), exposing internal subject-predicate structure and enabling general claims over domains—something propositional logic (which treats sentences as indivisible units) cannot express.

column1: What three components constitute a first-order structure ⟨D, I⟩?
column2: A non-empty domain of discourse D, plus an interpretation I that maps individual constants to domain elements, n-ary predicates to sets of n-tuples from D, and n-ary function symbols to operations on D.

column1: State the Compactness Theorem and give its paradoxical implication.
column2: If every finite subset of a set of premises is satisfiable, then the entire (possibly infinite) set is satisfiable. Paradox: an infinite set of sentences asserting 'at least n objects exist' for all n has only finite models for each finite subset, yet compactness guarantees a model (necessarily infinite) for the whole set.

column1: What is the key limitation of Gödel's Completeness Theorem regarding logic order?
column2: It holds only for first-order logic; second-order and higher-order logics lack completeness—there exist truths that no recursively enumerable rule set can derive.

column1: What are the two core components of a Kripke frame in modal logic?
column2: A non-empty set W of possible worlds, and a binary accessibility relation R on W, where R(w, w') means world w' is accessible/possible relative to world w.

column1: What is the core invariant that modal logic adds beyond classical bivalence?
column2: Truth becomes relative to possible worlds: a proposition can be true in some worlds and false in others, while each world itself retains classical bivalence (true/false with no middle ground).

column1: What is Brouwer's intuitionist objection to the Law of Excluded Middle (P ∨ ¬P)?
column2: Mathematical truth requires constructive proof; asserting P ∨ ¬P demands either a proof of P or a proof of ¬P. Since many propositions lack either, excluded middle cannot be a universal logical law under constructivism.
